title: Calendar and invites
brief: People view their week, create meetings and invite others. Each invite sends an email or phone alert. Monday at 9 am everyone opens the calendar at once. A repeated send must never produce two invites, and a slow email partner must not slow the calendar.

clarify.a: Within a minute is fine. The calendar page itself must be quick.

clarify.q: What if the email partner limits us?
clarify.a: It will, at busy times. Alerts wait in a line and go out when the partner allows.

clarify.q: What if a message is delivered twice?
clarify.a: The guest must still see one invite, so each invite carries a unique key.

notes: About 144 new meetings a second at the Monday peak (approx.).
On a busy morning the email partner slows to a few dozen messages a second (approx.).
Notification speed measures provider acceptance. Device receipt is outside this traffic model; check expiry, provider outcome and retries in the correctness trace before claiming delivery guarantees.

numbers.how: At 40 percent of the 36 a second, so a line forms and drains later (approx.)

hints: The email partner slows down at 9 am. Where do the extra alerts wait?
A queue holds alerts and workers send them at the pace the partner allows. A key on each invite makes a repeat harmless.
Load balancer, servers, cache for views, SQL database, idempotency store, queue, workers, email provider.

editorial.summary: Viewing is a cached read. Creating an invite is a write plus a promise of an alert. The alert goes on a queue so the calendar never waits for the partner, and a unique key makes every repeat harmless.

designs.name: Queue the alerts, key every invite
designs.why: The server saves the meeting, then puts the alert on a queue and answers at once. Workers send at the partner's pace, and the idempotency store drops repeated deliveries.

tradeoffs: A short cache time keeps the week view fresh. A long one saves the database but shows a stale meeting.
A queue means an alert may be a minute late. That is the price of never blocking the calendar.
Unique keys cost a lookup but turn a repeated delivery into a no-op.
If the partner is down for long, a second provider is a cheap way to keep alerts moving.
editorial.realWorld: Calendar systems see their biggest bursts on Monday mornings, when millions of people open the week at once. Alerts are sent through outside email and push partners with their own limits (approx.).

correctness.prompt: A worker sends a message, then crashes before recording success. What key and delivery states would you store so a retry does not send it twice?
correctness.discussion: Give each logical message a stable key, scoped to its recipient and channel, and enforce a unique constraint on that key. Save the request and an outbox entry in one transaction, then track pending, sending and delivered states. A queue alone does not prevent duplicates. If the provider accepts the send but the worker crashes, retry with the same provider idempotency key or query its status. Without provider support, exactly-once external delivery cannot be guaranteed: discuss whether a possible duplicate or a possible missed message is acceptable.

fields.label: The provider accepts the operation, then the worker crashes before saving success. What state is durable?
options: Unknown outcome, with the original logical operation key
Failed, so the retry gets a new key
fields.explanation: Missing local success does not prove the provider rejected the operation.

fields.label: The queue redelivers that operation. What can establish one external effect?
options: Check a local cache, then send without a provider key
Reuse the provider idempotency key or reconcile its recorded outcome
fields.explanation: A local lookup and a remote side effect are not atomic. Without endpoint support, one external effect cannot be guaranteed; report uncertainty and choose an explicit recovery policy.

twist.brief: Demand has settled at about 300 requests/s. The new monthly ceiling is $2,500. The original burst reserve now competes with the operating budget. Decide which reserve to keep, then test its failure headroom. All data and recovery promises still apply.

design.name: Smaller workload, measured reserve
design.why: Reduce the paid floor for the quieter workload, preserving the required copies and recovery settings. This design was checked through the full event day.
